The American mink (Neogale vison) is a semi-aquatic mustelid with a suite of life-history traits finely tuned to its riparian and wetland habitats. Gestation, including a period of embryonic diapause, lasts approximately 42 days [tg = approximately 42 days] when measured under typical captive conditions at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a duration that aligns closely with that of other medium-sized mustelids. Neonatal mink emerge from the birth canal weighing only about 5.8 grams [Wwb = about 5.8 grams], an altricial birth mass that reflects the relatively short intrauterine development period and the subsequent intensive parental investment required to rear the vulnerable pups. This low mass at parturition necessitates a substantial allocation of maternal resources during the ensuing lactation phase, which proceeds under the same thermoneutral conditions of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] commonly maintained in research colonies.

This phase of rapid mass gain is fueled entirely by the mother's milk, and the transition to solid food marks a critical period of nutritional independence. The 49-day weaning age is relatively brief compared to some larger carnivores, yet it is sufficiently long to allow the kits to develop the hunting skills necessary for a piscivorous and carnivorous diet once they leave the natal den.

The maximum lifespan recorded for American mink, under the consistently warm conditions of a captive environment maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], is approximately 4,161 days [am = approximately 4,161 days], equivalent to roughly 11.4 years. This longevity is relatively extended for a mammal of its body size and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by a predator-free captive setting. Adult body size is strongly sexually dimorphic; the ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 700 grams [Wwi = approximately 700 grams], while males achieve a much greater asymptotic mass of around 1,300 grams [Wwi = around 1,300 grams], a difference that facilitates their divergent roles in territorial defense and mating competition. Basal metabolic rate in Neogale vison, determined through respirometry on post-absorptive individuals at rest within their thermoneutral zone of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], reaches 488 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 488 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively high oxygen consumption, when scaled against the species' adult body mass, is characteristic of a mustelid with an elongated, streamlined body plan and a high surface-area-to-volume ratio that promotes heat loss in its aquatic foraging environment. Comparative studies of related mustelids such as the European polecat and the long-tailed weasel indicate that the mink's combination of a relatively long lifespan, delayed sexual maturation in males, and moderate fecundity positions it as a slow-to-medium life-history strategist within the mustelid family, well suited to the seasonal and resource-pulsed dynamics of its freshwater habitats.
